newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: El Nino drought seen hitting Australia beef market.
newsitem.headline: El Nino drought seen hitting Australia beef market.

text.p: Frosts and fears of an El Nino drought boosted the number of store cattle for sale in Australia in recent months, depressing prices, the Australian Meat and Livestock Corp (AMLC) said on Wednesday.
Prices for slaughter-ready stock rose in June, encouraged by tightening supplies of good quality, slaughter-ready cattle, the AMLC said in its latest Australian Meat and Livestock Review.
Cattle prices gained momentum in July from a general improvement in export markets, posting further moderate gains, it said.
Cow prices held firm despite a large increase in supplies.
But a deterioration in prices for stock in store condition contrasted with this, the AMLC said.
"As frosts impacted on pasture conditions and warnings sounded of the possibility of another El Nino event, the number of store cattle offered for sale increased," it said.
This made graziers cautious participants in the market.

A large rise in April slaughter figures, an extremely large May kill, continued large throughputs in New South Wales (NSW) and Queensland during June and record live cattle exports had confirmed Australian turnoff through the first half of 1997 as the largest since the drought of 1992, it said.
The rise in slaughter levels had been almost entirely because of the increased female kill, with the cow and heifer kill up by 20 percent compared with the same period of last year, the AMLC said.
"These factors are undeniable indicators of considerable herd liquidation," it said.
Severe drought in southern Australia and worsening conditions in northern areas was one reason for this.

Other reasons included a continuation of poor cattle prices, financial pressures and cash flow considerations, the possibility of another El Nino drought event and a slightly more optimistic outlook for wool, it said.
"Although slaughter levels should ease seasonally in July/August, unless widespread rain is received or cattle prices rise substantially, kills will most likely remain above a year ago," it said.
Output was currently about 7.5 percent above last year but with the large increase in the cow kill, much of the rise was in the lean end of the market, suited for further processing.
A feedlot survey showed numbers in feedlots rising steadily in the June quarter, to 480,000 head, mainly because of increased feeding for the domestic market, the AMLC said.
September quarter numbers were expected to fall back to the 447,000 level of the March quarter, it said.
This reflected an anticipated improvement in seasonal conditions in the south of Australia during the spring, which reduced the domestic market's requirement for grainfed beef.
June exports, although down on May, remained well above year-ago volumes at 68,000 tonnes, up 13,000 tonnes on June 1996, the AMLC said.
Shipments to Japan totalled 26,800 tonnes, down on the healthy May level of 29,400 tonnes.

However, June exports to South Korea rose substantially to 4,200 tonnes from 1,600 tonnes a year before because of success by Australian exporters in the Livestock Products Marketing Organisation tender at the end of May, the AMLC said.
-- Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
